analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. carbon emissions and pays the permit auction proceeds out as equal cash dividends to every legal resident.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2009 with 4 cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a declining limit on the amount of oil, natural gas, and coal that could be burned in the United States, cutting emissions to 85% below 2005 levels by 2050. Companies that first sell fossil fuels into U.S. markets would have to buy carbon permits at public auctions to cover the emissions from the fuels they sell. All of that auction money would go into a trust fund and be paid out in equal monthly dividends to every person lawfully in the United States with a valid Social Security number. It also would have charged a fee on carbon-heavy imports like steel and cement, so foreign producers could not undercut U.S. firms that face the carbon cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Every lawfully present U.S. resident with a Social Security number would receive an equal monthly dividend from the permit auction proceeds. Because each person gets the same amount while wealthier households typically burn more fossil fuel, lower- and middle-income households would come out ahead on net. Households and businesses would also gain from slower climate change and cleaner air.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every lawful U.S. resident, especially lower earners

how_it_helps.text: All proceeds from the carbon permit auctions and any penalties flow into a Healthy Climate Trust Fund and are paid out as equal monthly dividends to each eligible individual, with administrative costs capped at 0.5% [S3].
The emissions cap tightens on a fixed schedule: 25% below 2005 emissions by 2020, 45% by 2030, 65% by 2040, and 85% by 2050 [S2].

The bill prevents companies from hoarding or speculating in permits by limiting how many a single entity can buy or hold, and sets a stiff penalty of three times market value for failing to surrender permits [S3].

Border fees on carbon-intensive imports (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, chemicals, paper) keep foreign producers without carbon costs from displacing U.S. producers, and rebates go to U.S. exporters [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, natural gas, and coal companies that first sell fossil fuels in U.S. markets would pay for permits covering the carbon in everything they sell. Importers of carbon-intensive goods would pay equivalence fees. Some of those costs would pass through to consumers as higher fuel and goods prices, though the equal dividend is designed to more than offset the average household's added cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel sellers and carbon-intensive importers

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel costs would pass through to consumers as higher prices for gasoline, heating, and electricity, and the monthly dividend would lag behind price spikes, squeezing households in the transition [S3].
Coal-dependent regions and workers whose livelihoods rest on fossil fuel production would bear concentrated losses, and the bill contains no specific transition assistance for them [S2].
The border fee mechanism would raise prices on imported steel, cement, and other goods, and could invite trade disputes with countries that do not adopt equivalent carbon policies [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually direct: every dollar raised from the carbon charge goes back out as an equal per-person payment, so the average household, especially lower-income ones, comes out ahead financially while emissions fall. The real costs fall on fossil fuel producers and on households in the transition period before dividends catch up to higher prices, and on coal-region workers with no dedicated transition help in the bill. It is a strong design on paper; the honest objection is the transition pain and the uncertainty of how permit prices would behave.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, was sent to an Energy and Environment subcommittee two days after introduction, and never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Van Hollen introduced the Cap and Dividend Act of 2009 on April 1, 2009, joined by Reps. Thompson of California, Blumenauer, and Doggett [S3].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, the Energy and Commerce Committee; it drew 4 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1].

On April 2, 2009, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Environment, and the record shows no further action — no markup, no vote, and no floor consideration through the end of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers of carbon-intensive goods are better off because the bill died: they avoided a new carbon cost on every ton of oil, gas, and coal sold. Ordinary people lost the chance at equal monthly dividend checks funded by those charges.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and carbon-intensive importers

sides.party_line_note: Only 4 of 253 House Democrats signed on and no Republican supported it; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where either party stood.

industries.industry: Oil, natural gas, and coal producers and first sellers
industries.note: They would have to buy permits for the carbon in every unit of fuel they sell, a direct cost scaled to their output. Their gain from the bill's failure was the avoidance of that cost, which the bill would have redistributed to the public as dividends.

industries.industry: U.S. heavy manufacturing (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: Domestic producers would pay permit costs embedded in energy but receive export rebates and border fees against foreign competitors without carbon costs, largely shielding them. Consumers would face the fee on carbon-intensive imports.
A tightening cap would steadily raise fossil fuel costs, making wind, solar, and efficiency investments more competitive. No direct subsidy, just a changing price landscape.
